title: How many CPUs does this machine have, really?
summary: Packages, cores and hardware threads, the caches each one shares, hybrid cores, and how Linux numbers logical CPUs and groups them for the scheduler.

version_notes.text: /sys/devices/system/cpu/smt/control and smt/active, added with the L1TF mitigations, report and switch simultaneous multithreading at run time.
topology/die_id and die_cpus_list describe dies, for packages that hold more than one.
On hybrid Intel processors /sys/devices/cpu_core/cpus and /sys/devices/cpu_atom/cpus list the performance and efficiency cores, because the two kinds have different performance counters.
topology/cluster_id and cluster_cpus_list describe clusters of cores that share an L2 cache or other resources below the package level.

For thirty years a faster computer meant a faster clock. Around 2005 that stopped: each smaller transistor still switched faster, but no longer at lower power, and a chip that runs faster than about 4 GHz turns too much of its power into heat to cool. What kept growing was the number of transistors. Designers spent them on more complete processors on one chip, called
, each able to run its own program.
A single core is also idle more often than it looks. When an instruction waits a hundred nanoseconds for memory, the execution units behind it have nothing to do.

(SMT; Intel calls it Hyper-Threading) gives one core two sets of registers, so it can run two instruction streams and fill one stream's stalls with the other's work. To the operating system each set looks like a separate processor.

So a modern machine is a nest: packages hold cores, cores hold hardware threads, and caches are shared at every level in between. Linux schedules onto the innermost unit, the hardware thread, and calls each one a

. But where a task runs matters: two tasks on sibling threads compete for one core, a task moved to another core leaves its cached data behind, and on some processors one core is simply faster than another. The scheduler needs the nest, and the kernel publishes it.
is what sits in a socket. It may contain several
(separate pieces of silicon, such as the chiplets of an AMD Ryzen or EPYC), each die several
, and each core one or more

. Firmware describes this nest to the kernel at boot: x86 processors report it through the CPUID instruction (leaves 0xB and 0x1F) and the ACPI tables, arm64 systems through the MPIDR register, ACPI's PPTT table or the device tree.

The kernel numbers the logical CPUs in the order firmware lists them, and that order rarely matches the nest. Intel and AMD desktops usually list the first thread of every core before any second thread, so CPU 0 and CPU
-core part, not CPU 0 and CPU 1. Each CPU's directory in
. Only the sibling list identifies a core reliably: core ids are labels that can repeat in every package and skip numbers.

Sibling threads have separate registers and instruction pointers, and share almost everything else: the decoders, the execution units, the L1 and L2 caches and the core's TLB. When one thread stalls on memory the other uses the idle units, which typically adds 10 to 30 percent of throughput to the core, far from doubling it. When both are busy with the same kind of work, each runs noticeably slower than it would alone.

Sharing also leaks. Several speculative-execution attacks, such as L1TF and MDS, let one thread infer data the sibling thread touched in shared buffers. That is why the kernel can switch SMT off at run time:

Each core has its own small, fast L1 caches, one for data and one for instructions, a few tens of kilobytes answering in about a nanosecond. Behind them is a larger L2, private to a core on most designs and shared by a cluster of four cores on others (Intel's efficiency cores, many arm designs). The last level, L3, is megabytes in size and shared by all the cores of a package or of one chiplet. Caches move memory in lines of 64 bytes.

Some processors mix cores of different designs: large
cores (Intel since Alder Lake; arm's big.LITTLE and DynamIQ). The scheduler must then place demanding tasks on fast cores and background work on slow ones. The kernel describes the difference as a

What the scheduler builds from it
At boot, and whenever CPUs come or go, the scheduler builds

: nested groups of CPUs that share something. Typically the smallest domain is the SMT siblings of one core, the next the cores sharing a cache, then the package, then NUMA nodes. Each row is one physical cache. A level with as many rows as cores is private to each core; a level with one row per package is shared by the whole package.

Atlas found evidence of a virtual machine. Every figure above is the topology the hypervisor chose to present: the "cores" are threads of the host scheduled like any other, they may move between physical cores, and two of them may share one physical core without either knowing.

The figures above are what the kernel was told at boot. On bare metal they describe the silicon; inside a virtual machine, which Machine Atlas found no evidence of here, they would describe whatever the hypervisor chose to present.
Whether this system is a virtual machine could not be determined here. If it is, every figure above is the topology the hypervisor chose to present, not the physical cores underneath.
Two programs each keep one hardware thread busy with arithmetic and little memory traffic. Will they finish sooner on two sibling threads of one core, or on two different cores?

options.s: Sooner on siblings: they share a cache, so they help each other.
Sooner on different cores: siblings compete for one core's execution units.
No difference: a logical CPU is a CPU.

inl.s: On different cores. Sibling threads share the execution units, so two arithmetic-heavy programs on one core each get roughly the share of the core the other leaves, typically 55 to 65 percent of their speed alone; on two cores each runs at full speed. The scheduler knows this, which is why it fills idle cores before idle siblings.

The first answer is right for a different workload: two threads exchanging data through memory can benefit from sharing a core's L1 and L2, because a cache line written by one is already where the other reads it. The third is what the logical CPU count invites you to believe.

On a machine with SMT you can measure the prediction. Pick two siblings from the table above and two CPUs on different cores, and time the same busy loop pinned each way:

blocks.label: general
blocks.text: time (taskset -c 0 sh -c 'i=0; while [ $i -lt 3000000 ]; do i=$((i+1)); done' & taskset -c SIBLING sh -c 'i=0; while [ $i -lt 3000000 ]; do i=$((i+1)); done' & wait)

inl.s: Replace SIBLING with cpu0's sibling, then with a CPU on another core. Expect the pair on one core to take noticeably longer; on a busy machine the difference is noisier.

blocks.title: nproc is the number of cores

inl.s: counts the logical CPUs this process may run on: hardware threads, after affinity and cpusets have removed any. On a machine with SMT it is twice the number of cores; in a container with a CPU set it can be fewer than the machine has; and it ignores CPU quotas entirely.

Two hardware threads share one core's execution units and caches. They add throughput only where one thread leaves units idle, typically 10 to 30 percent, and two busy siblings each run slower than one thread alone.

blocks.label: general
blocks.title: Neighbouring CPU numbers are neighbours on the chip

inl.s: Logical CPU numbers follow the order firmware lists the threads, which on most x86 machines puts all first threads before all second threads. Siblings, dies and packages must be read from the topology files, never inferred from the numbers.

Nothing here measures distance or speed. The topology says which CPUs share a core or a cache, not how long a cache line takes to travel between them, how hot each core runs, or how a hybrid core's speed compares beyond the capacity number the kernel was given.
Inside a virtual machine the topology is a description chosen by the hypervisor, and nothing inside the guest can see the physical cores its virtual CPUs run on or which other guests share them.
The physical arrangement on the die, which cores sit next to which cache slice, is not published at all.
follows how fast each of these cores is allowed to run, and why that changes from moment to moment. In Explore, the
components show what depends on this nest. Planned lessons cover CPU caches and cache lines in depth, NUMA placement, and how the scheduler's domains balance load between cores.
